10532-beacon-lights-of-history-volume-06:
John Lord published this sixth volume of Beacon Lights of History, on the Renaissance and Reformation, in a later numbering that puts subjects in historical order. An earlier set had numbered the same lectures differently, by the order in which Lord gave them. The volume treats the rebirth of learning and the break with Rome.

Dante opens the set, with modern poetry, his banishment, Guelphs and Ghibellines, and his love for Beatrice, leading to the Divine Comedy. Later lectures will follow other makers of the age. Readers get a readable, moral history of a turning age, through its great poets and reformers.
11242-the-life-of-michelangelo-buonarrot:
John Addington Symonds's life of Michelangelo follows the artist from birth and boyhood in Florence through Lorenzo de' Medici's death, first visits to Bologna and Rome, and the David in Florence. Later chapters cover Julius II's tomb project, the Sistine vault, the Medici sacristy and library, the sack of Rome, the Last Judgment, and Michelangelo's final years as architect-in-chief at St. Peter's. Separate chapters assess him as draughtsman, painter, sculptor, architect, and poet.

Symonds, a Victorian scholar of the Renaissance, writes with admiration and ample documentation, including friendships with Vittoria Colonna and Tommaso Cavalieri. The biography is long and detailed, suited to readers who want a full life rather than a short appreciation. It remains a standard nineteenth-century account of its subject.
11728-abraham-lincoln-the-people-s-leade:
George Haven Putnam's 1909 book, Abraham Lincoln: The People's Leader in the Struggle for National Existence, opens on the centenary of Lincoln's birth, 12 February 1909. New York and other cities marked the day, and even Atlanta heard Southern testimony to Lincoln's life.

Chapters cover the evolution of the man, work at the bar, entrance into politics, and the fight against the extension of slavery. The volume includes Lincoln's New York speech of 27 February 1860, with an introduction by Charles C. Nott. Later pages weigh the soldiers' vote in 1864 and Chase's habit of threatening resignation.
11977-the-united-empire-loyalists-a-chro:
W. Stewart Wallace's United Empire Loyalists, volume 13 of the Chronicles of Canada edited by George M. Wrong and H. H. Langton, appeared in Toronto in 1914. Its contents move from loyalism in the thirteen colonies and persecution of the loyalists to the loyalists under arms, peace without honour, and the exodus to Nova Scotia and beyond.

Wallace tells the story of Americans who stayed loyal to Britain during the Revolution and paid for it with exile, loss, and resettlement in Canada. The chronicle treats the great migration as a founding event for Canada, shaping its politics, society. Identity in ways that still echoed when Wallace wrote on the eve of the First World War.
12002-review-of-the-work-of-mr-john-stua:
George Grote's 1868 Review of John Stuart Mill's Examination of Sir William Hamilton's Philosophy reprints his Westminster Review article of January 1, 1866. Grote, author of the History of Ancient Greece and Plato and the Other Companions of Socrates, examines Mill's attack on Hamilton and the principal philosophical questions discussed in Mill's book.

The review treats Mill's arguments on perception, causation, and the limits of knowledge with the care of a fellow philosopher and historian. For readers of Victorian thought, it shows two major minds in conversation: Mill challenging the Scottish common-sense school. Grote weighing whether Mill's criticism succeeds on its own terms.
13986-speech-of-mr-cushing-of-massachuse:
Caleb Cushing of Massachusetts spoke in the House on January 25, 1836, on the right of petition. He held several petitions on slavery in the District of Columbia and moved that one be received. The petition prayed for abolition of slavery and the slave trade in the district. Gales and Seaton printed the speech in Washington.

Cushing warns that refusing reception would abridge a great right inherent in the people. He places responsibility on those raising this novel question of reception. The speech belongs to the gag-rule debates that gripped Congress. It shows a Northern congressman defending petition against Southern pressure. The text suits students of antebellum politics.
14019-the-harvard-classics-volume-49-epi:
Edited by Charles W. Eliot in 1910, this Harvard Classics volume pairs two early epics: the Song of Roland and the Destruction of Dá Derga's Hostel. John O'Hagan's Roland retells the rear-guard disaster at Roncesvaux in 778, when Frankish forces marching through the Pyrenees were cut down by Basque attackers. Roland's pride, his horn, and his dying stand anchor the French poem.

Irish saga supplies the second half. King Conaire, bound by sacred taboos, walks toward a fated hostel where omens pile up: strange guests, huge figures, and a swineherd's welcome that turns ominous. Notes and introductions frame both works for general readers. Together they show how two cultures sang of doomed kings and loyal companions, and why Eliot placed heroic story at the heart of a liberal education.
15263-the-underground-railroad-a-record-:
William Still's 1872 record of the Underground Railroad gathers facts, narratives, and letters on slaves' hardships, hairbreadth escapes, and death struggles for freedom. Still, long of Philadelphia's Anti-Slavery Office and chair of its Vigilant Committee, saw much of it himself. Seventy engravings and photo portraits enrich the book.

Stories told by fugitives and their helpers sit beside sketches of large stockholders and liberal aiders of the road. A Deuteronomy motto on not returning an escaped servant fronts the work. The book stands as a monumental firsthand source for the freedom struggle, essential for American history.
1601-conversation-as-it-was-by-the-socia:
Mark Twain imagines an evening in the time of the Tudors, when great ladies and gentlemen sit by the fire and talk with a frankness no Victorian drawing room allowed. The introduction quotes his own scratch-pad line: born irreverent, he hoped to remain so. It also tells how he once sent the piece, unsigned, to an editor who had cried out for a new Rabelais — and got it savagely abused.

The talk ranges over the customs, learning, and scandal of Queen Elizabeth's court, in language Twain delighted to make as broad as the age itself. He printed the sketch privately for friends in his lifetime. It stands as his bawdiest jeu d'esprit, learned and improper in equal measure.
16127-the-diamond-cross-mystery-being-a-:
Chester K. Steele's 1918 detective novel, issued by the International Fiction Library in Cleveland, opens on a grim April morning in a jewelry shop. The only sound in the stillness is the ticking of a watch in the hand of a dead woman, while rain falls outside. Chapters with titles like The Ticking Watch, King's Dagger, The Fisherman, Spotty, and The Diamond Cross promise a winding case.

A colonel, a young woman named Amy, a searcher named Grafton, and a string of odd clues, coins, and hidden wires keep the plot moving through twenty-two chapters. Steele, author of The Mansion of Mystery, writes brisk popular mystery with a fresh twist in each chapter. Readers who like old-style whodunits will enjoy its pace and surprises.
19029-the-gifts-of-asti:
Andrew North wrote this short science fantasy tale, first printed in Fantasy Book in 1948. Varta, last of the virgin maidens of Asti, flees a burning city with Lur, a scaled creature who speaks to her mind. Her world is dead, and she must lead what remains to a new land.

They cross jungle, glassy slag deserts left by war, and green valleys where Asti's gifts still grow. Fruit, prey, and old roads mark their path, while barbarian hordes press behind them. Readers get a vivid tale of flight, faith, and a guardian's last duty to her people.
19424-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Percy Addleshaw wrote this guide to Exeter Cathedral for Bell's cathedral series, with many pictures. It tells the history of the bishop's see and the building. Then it walks the reader through its fabric in plain terms, from the long unbroken roof line to the tombs and chantries inside.

Small human details give the guide life, such as bequests for yearly masses and the stark epitaph on a bishop's tomb. Like its sister volumes, it was made for ordinary visitors who want true facts and clear sightlines, not a scholar's treatise, and it still works on a visit today.
19900-the-mysteries-of-all-nations-rise-:
James Grant's Mysteries of All Nations traces the rise and progress of superstition. He confesses his examples come from an almost unlimited number. Many interesting particulars had to be omitted, he says. A friend's letter from Macroom, Ireland, arrived even as the last sheet was revised. It corroborated his Irish material handsomely. Grant piles custom upon custom across nations and centuries.

Victorian rationalists loved cataloging the beliefs they opposed. Charms, omens, witch trials, and holy frauds fill such surveys. Grant writes as a journalist, brisk and anecdotal. Modern readers can mine him for folklore he scorned. Ireland, Scotland, and farther lands all supply cases. The book is a museum of nineteenth-century unbelief.
20191-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
J. E. Bygate wrote the Bell's Cathedrals volume on the cathedral church of Durham. Bygate draws much of the account from his own time in the building. He also used Greenwell's pamphlet and Ross's County of Durham. Those sources add depth on one of England's greatest Norman churches.

Durham Cathedral crowns its rock above the River Wear in bold mass. The book describes its nave, shrine, towers, and long past in order. Bell's series made each great church plain to tourists and students. Readers get a compact guide rich in stone, story, and saint lore.
20641-through-three-campaigns-a-story-of:
G. A. Henty built his boys' novel Through Three Campaigns out of three real British campaigns. The relief of Chitral, the Tirah campaign, and the relief of Coomassie in Ashanti supply the action. Henty's heroes serve as young officers and learn soldiering on three frontiers.

The first two campaigns, Henty notes, were fought in mountainous country. The ground gave every advantage to the enemy, since passes had to be scaled and torrents crossed under fire. The Ashanti fighting moved through forest instead. Henty mixes exact military detail with adventure, in the style that made him the boys' historian of the empire.
20810-the-ladies-of-llangollen-as-sketch:
About 1778, two ladies quit gay society to seek a secluded life together. Their search for a fitting spot led them to Llangollen in Wales. There they planned days of friendship, charity, and quiet good works.

Lady Eleanor Butler and Sarah Ponsonby became famed as the Ladies of Llangollen. Poets, lords, and travellers beat a path to their cottage door. This sketch, drawn by many hands, gathers views of their odd, admired life. Readers meet two women who built a celebrated home on their own terms, against the grain of their age.
20832-campfire-girls-at-twin-lakes-or-th:
Laughter, a bit scornful, greets Katherine Crane's riddle-like speech at Twin Lakes. Eleven girls of Flamingo Camp Fire form an arc on the grass before her. White tents dot the hillside camp in this Campfire Girls tale.

A summer vacation quest drives the plot, with lake, woods, and camp craft in play. Stella Francis, who wrote such tales, filled them with hikes and good deeds. The Camp Fire movement's laws of health and service shape each scrape. Young readers got both fun and a model of sturdy, kind girlhood in these brisk outdoor tales.
23291-sinks-of-london-laid-open-a-pocket:
This pocket companion lays open the sinks of London, a true picture of low city life for the uninitiated. Common lodging houses, cadgers, and St. Giles, the cadgers' headquarters, open a tour of beggars, thieves, and slang.

A modern flash dictionary adds every cant word and flash phrase then in vogue, with a list of sixty orders of prime coves. The book served the curious as both guide and glossary to a London most readers never saw. The flash dictionary turns slang into a guide for the curious reader. A beggar's repast chapter and an evening meal fit for an alderman show the sinks' strange feasts.
24935-famous-tales-of-fact-and-fancy-myt:
Logan Marshall's 1914 collection, translated and edited for young readers and published by Winston, gathers the great myths and legends of the ancient world in one volume. Prometheus and the Labors of Hercules open the heroic sequence, followed by Deucalion's flood, the adventures of Theseus, and the sorrows of Niobe. Hawthorne's telling of the Gorgon's Head brings Perseus to life for children.

Jason's quest for the Golden Fleece, with its brazen bulls, stands beside the Cyclops, Oedipus, Antigone, Iphigenia, and the Sack of Troy. Marshall keeps the stories swift and clear, trimming the horrors without losing their grandeur. For a young reader's first tour of Greek myth, the book remains a sturdy and generous guide.
24945-mufti:
Herman Cyril McNeile, writing as 'Sapper,' published Mufti with Hodder and Stoughton in 1919, a novel of wartime England and the men coming home from France. The prologue opens far from glory. An officer dozes in a homemade chair while a fat quartermaster-sergeant snores nearby, and an old warrior clears a drain as field punishment, finding a dead dog in it. A sausage balloon floats above the camp, and peace, not battle, sets the keynote.

The story moves to Rumfold Hall, where Joan Devereux keeps her distance from the hero, their meetings confined to commonplace remarks in company. Between scenes he reads First Men in the Moon for excitement and Ann Veronica for its rumored immorality. McNeile mixes comedy, romance, and the awkward return to civilian life with a soldier's eye.
25574-recollections-of-dante-gabriel-ros:
T. Hall Caine recalls Dante Gabriel Rossetti in this 1883 volume from Roberts Brothers. Caine's preface quotes Rossetti near the close of 1881, very ill, remembering how their correspondence began and how little he foresaw the relations that followed.

Rossetti, solitary and depressed at the time, found solace in letters from a young, ardent well wisher unknown to him in person. His letters to Caine, among the largest bodies of literary letters he ever wrote, kept almost wholly to literary subjects. Caine, told the choice would one day be his, prints recollections and letters from that friendship.
26137-starlight-ranch-and-other-stories-:
Captain Charles King's 1891 volume holds five stories of army life on the American frontier, copyrighted in 1890. The title story follows a scouting party high in the mountains. It hunts renegade Apaches across the Matitzal range and the Tonto Basin with keen-eyed Indian allies. Later tales move between the plains and West Point, which the soldiers call the Point.

Other stories cover a troop's worst man, a character named Van, and the rough, loyal life of officers and men far from home. King wrote as a serving officer, and his tales mix bivouac talk, sudden danger, and barrack humour. The book gives a vivid, first-hand flavour of frontier service in the last years of the Indian wars.
26697-principles-of-mining-valuation-org:
Herbert C. Hoover published this mining textbook with the McGraw-Hill Book Company at New York and London in 1909, first edition, fourth thousand. Hoover, a member of the American Institute of Mining Engineers and fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, condensed lectures delivered at Stanford and Columbia Universities. He aimed neither at the wholly ignorant nor at the long experienced.

Early chapters value copper, gold, lead, silver, tin, and zinc lode mines. They cover sampling, assay plans, averages, errors, and ore in sight. They also cover prospective value, depth extension, secondary enrichment, and recoverable percentage against metal prices and production costs. Later chapters treat redemption of capital, mines with little ore in sight, and development by tunnels and shafts. Hoover notes most shafts serve moderate depths of twenty-five hundred to three thousand feet, with greater depths demanding larger ventilation, pumping, and winding.
26980-frank-h-nelson-of-cincinnati:
Warren C. Herrick's 1945 life of Frank H. Nelson of Cincinnati, with a foreword by Charles P. Taft, follows a city clergyman who became his town's conscience. Herrick, once Nelson's assistant, traces him from his call to the ministry through his work among Cincinnati's poor.

Chapters show Nelson as shepherd to his flock, spokesman of the city's conscience, and a presence people came simply to be near. The book recalls a rector who climbed tenement stairs daily, spoke plainly on public questions, and left an afterglow that outlasted his last years.
27286-gas-and-oil-engines-simply-explain:
Walter C. Runciman wrote this short, fully illustrated handbook in 1905 as number 26 of the Model Engineer series, aimed at amateurs and engine attendants rather than trained engineers. It explains in plain terms how gas and oil engines are built and run, with chapters on parts, ignition, governing, and valve settings.

The book opens with a brief history, from a gunpowder machine sketched in 1678 to John Barber's 1791 patent for force from burning fuel in air. Then it works through how a gas engine fires, how magneto ignition works, and how oil engines differ. A reader with a small engine to tend gets a clear, practical grounding here.
27306-an-interesting-journal-of-abner-st:
Private Abner Stocking of Chatham, Connecticut, kept this journal of the distressing events of Col. Benedict Arnold's 1775 expedition against Quebec, and his relatives published it at Catskill, New York, in 1810. The present text reprints that first printing, as extra number 75 of the Magazine of History, issued by William Abbatt at Tarrytown in 1921.

Stocking's account is the fourth journal of the expedition to be reprinted in the series, after those of Dr. Senter, Captain Topham, and Private Morison. Like theirs, it keeps the plain voice of one soldier and the hard detail of the march. Readers get a ground-level view of a famous failed campaign, told by a man who lived through it.
28815-the-bridge-of-the-gods-a-romance-o:
F. H. Balch wrote this romance of Indian Oregon, first published in 1890 and reissued in a nineteenth edition in 1915 with pictures by L. Maynard Dixon. The story draws on a Native legend that a great natural bridge once spanned the Columbia River before it fell. Balch learned the legend by visiting Native people, hearing their stories, and questioning old pioneers, and his publishers praised the book for faithful pictures of Indian character.

The novel follows Native life in the far West with attention to homes, work, games, and conversation, wrapped in a romantic plot. Its lasting popularity came from both the story and its claim to real knowledge of the Columbia country. Modern readers should note its period viewpoint, but the book remains a well-known early attempt to put Pacific Northwest Native legend into American fiction.
29058-a-new-orchard-and-garden-or-the-be:
William Lawson wrote this early gardening book, A New Orchard and Garden, first published in 1618 and taken here from the 1631 edition. The volume also holds The Country Housewife's Garden, Simon Harwood's treatise on propagating plants, and The Husbandman's Fruitful Orchard. Lawson teaches the best way for planting and grafting, and for making any ground fit for a rich orchard, especially in the north of England.

The book covers herbs of common use, their virtues, seasons, profits, and ornaments, with knots, models for trees, and plots for ordering grounds and walks. The husbandry of bees, drawn from forty-eight years of experience, stands beside it. Readers get a landmark of English gardening prose, in old spelling kept faithful, and still practical in its advice.
29424-quotes-and-images-an-index-of-the-:
David Widger compiled this index to the complete Project Gutenberg quotes and images collection, gathering wit and wisdom from a wide shelf of authors. Its contents run from Jacques Casanova and Lord Chesterfield through Dumas, La Fontaine, Galsworthy, Holmes, and Howells. Lincoln's writings, Montaigne, Meredith, Motley, Parker, Pepys, Rousseau, Twain, and Maupassant follow, with Columbus and the French Academy's immortals beside them.

The index holds no new essays of its own; it maps where quotations and pictures from these writers can be found in the Gutenberg set. Readers can hunt a line, a face, or a scene without paging through whole books. For browsers, teachers, and quote hunters, it serves as a handy doorway into a large treasury of words and images.
30564-before-and-after-waterloo-letters-:
Edward Stanley, sometime Bishop of Norwich, writes the letters gathered in Before and After Waterloo, edited by Jane H. Adeane and Maud Grenfell and published in London in 1907. Letters date from 1802, 1814, and 1816, with a biographical sketch of Stanley, born 1780 and died 1849.

Chapters move from new France and old Europe to after Napoleon's fall and under the Bourbon flag, with echoes of past days at Alderley Rectory. An illustration quotes a French line about the Rhine courier losing all on return from the Leipzig fair. Stanley's letters give a bishop's eye view of war, peace, and European change.
31447-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Drawn from the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, this slice runs alphabetically from Chitral to Cincinnati. It gathers a wide range of entries, from places and peoples to ideas and institutions. Among the articles named in the transcriber's notes are Chopin, Christianity, Church History, and Ciborium, showing the breadth a single alphabetical run could hold.

Reference works of this kind aimed to give the educated reader a trustworthy summary of each subject in a few pages. The slice is useful today both for its facts and for its viewpoint, since it records what leading scholars of the early twentieth century thought worth saying. Readers can dip into single entries or read across the slice for a picture of the age.
3190-1601-conversation-as-it-was-by-the-:
Mark Twain imagines a Tudor fireside in this ribald jeu d'esprit, dated 1601. An introduction quotes his own note on his trade. Born irreverent, he writes, like all other people he ever knew, he hoped to stay so. He would stay so while any reverent irreverences were left to make fun of. The piece is his richest expression of that sovereign contempt for piety.

Elizabeth's court supplies the company, and the talk runs as broad as Twain dared make it. Queens, courtiers, and poets trade jests no history book would print. The work circulated privately in Twain's lifetime, too frank for his public. Behind the celebrity stands the humorist unbuttoned, laughing at reverence itself.
32276-poetical-works-comprising-elegies-:
J. Parkerson, Junior's Poetical Works, comprising elegies, sketches from life, pathetic and extempore pieces, was printed and sold in Norwich by Lane and Walker at St. Andrew's, priced at one shilling. It was sold also by the author, in London, in Yarmouth, and by all booksellers. The volume is a poet's shilling book, transcribed from an early copy.

Its opening poem, The Bankrupt, addresses a friend who prayed the poet in youth never to stray from truth's paths. Youth, the poet owns, was much too prone to vice. Induced to riot, swear, and game, he thought to acquire fame in vice, only to find riot's poisoning scenes robbing his mind of joy and quiet. Debt pressed on debt. He could not pay, and awoke to keen sorrow. Readers get a moralising verse book, where rake's progress ends in bankruptcy.
33419-evacuation-day-1783-its-many-stirr:
James Riker's Evacuation Day, 1783, tells of the British leaving New York, with recollections of Captain John Van Arsdale of the Veteran Corps of Artillery. Van Arsdale, whose actions that day outwitted the enemy, is shown in an illustration tearing down the British flag. Riker's account, priced at fifty cents, gathers the day's stirring events in plain, patriotic prose.

The book suits readers of Revolutionary history, offering a local, first-hand flavor of a famous farewell. Its value lies in its detail on the flag, the troops, and the city's joy. For students of New York history, Evacuation Day is a vivid, short record of a day when a new nation watched its old rulers sail away.
33498-bransford-of-rainbow-range-origina:
Eugene Manlove Rhodes tells a western story of cowboys, round-ups, and a siege in the New Mexico range country. Bransford, first published under the title Bransford in Arcadia, opens after the long fall round-up, when the wagon camps for a last night on the way home. From that campfire start the tale moves through disguises, an alibi, a siege at Double Mountain, flight, and a farewell.

Rhodes writes with humor and a cowboy's ear for speech, balancing adventure with reflection on loyalty and the passing of the open range. Eighteen chapters plus a prologue carry Bransford from the pitcher that went to the well to the rainbow's end. Readers of classic westerns will enjoy its mix of action, trickery, and affection for ranch life.
33978-the-aboriginal-population-of-alame:
S. F. Cook wrote this University of California study of native peoples in Alameda and Contra Costa counties, issued in 1957. Anthropological Records volume sixteen, number four, runs from page 131 to 156 with three maps. Cook traces Spanish expeditions first: Fages-Crespi, Anza-Font, and Canizares, with later trips by Danti, Amador, Peralta, Viader, and Abella.

A section on aboriginal groups gives locations and population estimates, with a bibliography to close. Cook weighs expedition journals and later records with care. The study serves students of California native history in two bay counties.
4602-the-kingdom-of-god-is-within-you-ch:
Count Leo Tolstoy wrote The Kingdom of God Is Within You as a work of Christian thought, translated from the Russian by Constance Garnett and published at New York in 1894. Its subtitle states its claim: Christianity not as a mystic religion, but as a new theory of life. Garnett's preface calls the book one of the most remarkable studies of the social and psychological condition of the modern world to appear in Europe for many years.

Tolstoy argues that Christ's teaching, taken plainly, forbids violence and reshapes how people should live, work, and obey the state. His later philosophical and religious works, Garnett notes, were much talked about because they were his, yet seldom seriously discussed. Readers get a challenging, earnest book that still provokes argument about faith, force, and conscience, and a key text for understanding Tolstoy after his novels.
6080-school-history-of-north-carolina-fr:
John W. Moore's School History of North Carolina, from 1584 to the present time, appears revised and enlarged in a fourteenth edition. At a session of the state Board of Education in November 1881, the board reserved the right to require further revisions of the work adopted for public schools.

Moore sought aid and counsel to perfect the book, thanking Mrs. C. P. Spencer, E. J. Hale, and Commissioner Montford McGehee, and above all Colonel W. L. Saunders, secretary of state, who aided assiduously in revision and through the press. The history serves teachers and pupils with a state story brought up to date.
7389-the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendel:
Between 1837 and 1848, Oliver Wendell Holmes moved from a young Boston poet to a public voice of his city. This volume gathers the additional poems of those years, outside the famous early lyrics. They include The Pilgrim's Vision, a song for Harvard's centennial, and a song written for the dinner given to Charles Dickens by the young men of Boston in 1842.

Other pieces mark the age's occasions: a steamboat wreck, a Berkshire jubilee, after-dinner verses, and a temperance dinner to which ladies were invited. Read in order, the poems show Holmes learning his craft in public, witty and sociable, with the doctor's eye for human nature already at work. The volume fills the gap between his first fame and his later breakfast-table essays.
9411-legends-of-the-gods-the-egyptian-te:
E. A. Wallis Budge edited and translated these legends of the Egyptian gods, published in London in 1912. Contents include the creation, the destruction of mankind, Ra and the snake-bite, and Horus of Edfu with the winged disk. The origin of Horus, Khensu and the princess of Bekhten, and a seven years' famine follow.

Plates show Horus spearing the hippopotamus fiend, and Isis with Osiris in classical accounts. Budge's texts open ancient Egypt to English readers. The book remains a key source for Egyptian myth, scholarly, vivid, and richly illustrated in its plates.
abraham-lincoln-the-people-s-leader-in-t: George Haven Putnam presents Abraham Lincoln as the people's leader in the fight for national existence in this 1909 volume. With the biography comes Lincoln's speech delivered at New York on February 27, 1860, introduced by Charles Nott and annotated by Nott and Cephas Brainerd. The introductory note recalls February 12, 1909, the hundredth anniversary of Lincoln's birth, kept in New York and even in Atlanta, whose capture in 1864 had signalled the Confederacy's collapse.
beacon-lights-of-history-volume-06-renai:
John Lord's sixth Beacon Lights volume joins the Renaissance to the Reformation. Dante opens it, under the heading Rise of Modern Poetry: the antiquity of poetry, the greatness of poets, and their influence on civilisation. Lord calls the true poet one of the rarest of men, and Dante his first modern witness.

Reformers close the argument. A peroration on Luther demands that each man interpret scripture for himself, by the light he has: private judgment revived, spiritual liberty restored, and the people emancipated from the Middle Ages. Conscience, persecution, and martyrdom are embraced in one breath. Whatever Lord's subject — painter, poet, or reformer — the lecture form stays the same: a great figure, a turning age, and a moral drawn in ringing periods for a lyceum audience.
bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-church-o:
Percy Addleshaw wrote this description of Exeter Cathedral's fabric and brief history of its see for Bell's cathedral series, with thirty-seven illustrations. Addleshaw, an Oxford man, follows the series plan: a walkable account for visitors that still serves students of archaeology. Bishops, chantries, and tombs punctuate the architecture.

One chantry endowment shows the medieval economy of prayer. The abbot and convent of St. Mary of Cleeve paid the Dean and Chapter six pounds, thirteen shillings and fourpence yearly to keep the obit of a benefactor and Canon Moore. Sylke's tomb nearby shows, in Addleshaw's words, a very ghostly figure, with the epitaph Sum quod eris, fueram quod es: I am what you will be; I was what you are. Pray for me, it asks, in the later Gothic manner.
britannica-1911-acoemeti:
Acoemeti were an order of Eastern monks. Their Greek name means sleepless. They celebrated divine service without pause. Prayer went on day and night. Communities split into choirs for the task. The choirs relieved one another in church by turns. Their first monastery arose on the Euphrates. That was early in the fifth century. One soon followed at Constantinople. The famous Studium monastery became their chief house there. So they were sometimes called Studites.

Controversy involved them deeply. They fought in the Christological disputes of two centuries. Those disputes concerned the nature of Christ. First they opposed Patriarch Acacius. He had sought compromise with the monophysites. Later they fell under censure themselves. The charge was Nestorian tendencies under Justinian. A like perpetual office existed at Agaunum. Its link to them is doubtful.
britannica-1911-agouti:
Agouti is the West Indian name of a rodent. Dasyprocta aguti is the species named here. It is the size of a rabbit roughly. Trinidad and Guiana are its home ground. Zoologists class it in the family Caviidae. About ten other Dasyprocta species share the name. All live in tropical America. Agoutis are slender-limbed with very short tails. Five front toes and three hind toes mark them. Their hair is coarse, especially on the hind-quarters.

Habits are nocturnal and forest-bound. Agoutis hide by day in hollow trunks. Burrows among roots shelter them too. Their pace is a trot or rapid springs. They swim well when they take to water. Leaves, roots, nuts, and fruits form their food. Plantations of sugar-cane and bananas suffer from them.
britannica-1911-basti:
Basti is a town and district of British India, in the Gorakhpur division of the United Provinces, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town, really a collection of villages, stands on the river Kuana, forty miles from Gorakhpur by railway, and held 14,761 people in 1901. It had no municipality of its own. The district around it is far larger, covering 2792 square miles of country in the same broad plain.

Wet land defines the district. It stretches out as one vast marshy plain, draining south-east and crossed by the Rapti, Kuana, Banganga, and four smaller rivers named in the entry. Between those streams lies rich alluvial soil, soil left by flooding rivers, often under water but producing good crops of rice, wheat, and barley. The district held 1,846,153 people in 1901. A railway crossed it, the Gogra river was navigable, transit trade with Nepal was large, and exports were chiefly rice and sugar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acta-pilati:
Acta Pilati, or the Gospel of Nicodemus, does not claim Pilate as author, but claims descent from official acts kept in the praetorium at Jerusalem. Its alleged Hebrew original is attributed to Nicodemus, while the title Gospel of Nicodemus is medieval. The apocryphon won wide credit in the Middle Ages and greatly shaped legends of the Passion. Its popularity shows in its many languages, each with two or more recensions: Greek, Coptic, Armenian, and Latin.

The Acta fall into three sections of uneven style. The first covers the trial of Jesus, based on Luke 23. The second covers the Resurrection. An appendix on the descent to hell is absent from the Greek text and later added. In it Leucius and Charinus, souls raised after the Crucifixion, tell the Sanhedrin of the Lord's descent to Limbo. Eusebius, well informed in 325, is cited on the work, and Lipsius and Dobschutz supply modern study.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alessandro-sc:
Alessandro Scarlatti was a Sicilian-born composer, born in 1659 at Trapani or Palermo and dead at Naples in October 1725. His tomb calls him music's restorer, and the entry credits him with originating the classical style of the eighteenth century and advancing concerted instrumental music. His first opera of 1679, Gli Equivoci nel Sembiante, was performed for Queen Christina of Sweden, and his career moved between Rome and Naples.

Scarlatti wrote more than a hundred operas, less than half surviving. He also wrote oratorios, motets, and innumerable chamber cantatas and serenades, plus organ, harpsichord, and other instrumental music. After serving at Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, he returned to Naples in 1708 or 1709 and lived there ten years. He then lived in Rome from 1718 to 1721 before dying at Naples. His distinction was to lay the foundation of the new style later perfected by Neapolitan and German composers, including Haydn, Mozart, and Beethoven.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alesso-baldov:
Alesso Baldovinetti was a Florentine painter, born in Florence in October 1427, dead there in August 1499. Born to a wealthy merchant father, he left the business and joined the Academy of St. Luke at twenty-one. He called himself a pupil of Paolo Uccello and, according to Vasari, taught the famous Ghirlandaio. He experimented with colour in fresco and oil, though his works survive badly preserved, and he ranked as his day's best mosaic worker.

Baldovinetti helped Andrea del Castagno and Domenico Veneziano with the lost frescoes of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence. Surviving works include a large Adoration of the Shepherds in the cloisters of Sant'Annunziata and the design for Domenico del Michelino's portrait of Dante in the duomo. His Holy Trinity Adored by Saints Gualberto and Benedetto, painted for Santa Trinità, now hangs in the Florence Academy. His Annunciation and Enthroned Virgin and Child hang in the Uffizi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-alciat:
Andrea Alciati, an Italian jurist, was born at Alzano, near Milan, in 1492 and died at Pavia in 1550. The only son of a Milanese ambassador to Venice, he studied law at Pavia and Bologna. In 1522 he published Paradoxa juris civilis, an explanation of the Greek terms in Roman law, a work he had composed at fifteen.

He became professor of law at Avignon in 1518, then at Bourges, and returned to Milan in 1538 as professor at Pavia, teaching at Milan, Bologna, and Ferrara. Paul III and Charles V honoured him as the first scholar of his age to dress barbarous legal learning with literary skill. His jurisprudence was collected at Padua in 1571 in six folio volumes, beside a posthumous history of Milan, his Responsa, a formula of the Roman empire, and epigrams. Today his Emblemata, metrical moral sayings in elegant diction, first edited at Augsburg in 1531, is his best-known work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anima-christi:
The Anima Christi is a well-known prayer from the early fourteenth century, enriched with indulgences by Pope John XXII in 1330. All manuscripts agree on these facts, so there can be no doubt of their exactness. As to authorship, it was perhaps written by John XXII. This is uncertain, since this pope has been falsely credited with similar compositions.

The prayer was long believed to be Saint Ignatius Loyola's, since he puts it in his Spiritual Exercises and often refers to it. This is a mistake: it appears in prayer books of the saint's youth and manuscripts before his birth in 1491. James Mearns found it in a British Museum manuscript of 1370. A prayer book of Cardinal Peter de Luxembourg, dead in 1387, contains it. The prayer was so well known in Ignatius's time that he only mentions it in the first edition, while later editions print it in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-lotti:
Venetian composer Antonio Lotti, born in 1667 and dead there in 1740, studied under Legrenzi and produced an opera, Il Giustino, written in his sixteenth year. He became second organist of St. Mark's in 1692, first organist in 1704, and maestro di cappella, or music director, in 1736, beating strong rivals for a post paying 400 ducats. Between 1703 and 1730 he wrote many masses and motets, short sacred choral pieces, above all a Miserere that replaced Legrenzi's setting and is still sung at St. Mark's each Holy Thursday.

He also wrote twenty-seven operas between 1693 and 1717 and spent two years at Dresden. After returning to Venice in November 1719, he abandoned secular writing and devoted himself to church and chamber music alone. A disputed madrigal, a part song, that Bononcini claimed as his own forms a famous incident, now generally judged to have wronged Bononcini.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aporti:
Italian educator and theologian Ferrante Aporti, born at San Martino dell'Argine in 1791 and dead at Turin in 1858, pioneered infant schools in Italy. After ordination and three years of study at Vienna, he became professor of church history at the Cremona seminary and superintendent of schools there. His special care was the schooling of poor children, and in 1827 he opened an infant school at Cremona for their benefit.

Success led to similar schools in other Italian cities, which Aporti visited in person. He encouraged teachers and published guides for them, including a manual for infant schools in 1833 and a primer in 1837. At the University of Turin he taught a course on teaching methods that drew many teachers. France made him a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour in 1846, Victor Emmanuel made him a senator in 1848, and in 1855 he became rector of Turin University.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-asti:
Asti, one of the districts of the region of Alexandria and suffragan of Turin, is a very old town that became Christian early in the Christian era. Its first known bishop was Pastor in 451, followed by Majoranus in 465, Benenatus in 680, and Evasius in 730. From 800 the regular bishops' list begins, though the see stood vacant from 1857 to 1867.

Some controversy surrounds the diocese's beginning and Evasius's episcopate, once placed by some at much older dates. Asti counts 182,600 Catholics, 107 parishes, and 300 secular priests, twelve regulars, ninety-two seminarians, and 525 churches or chapels. The entry is a compact diocesan record, joining an ancient town, a disputed early bishop, and a modern roll of parishes and clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-gabriel-po:
Blessed Gabriel Possenti, a Passionist student famed for holiness, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Assisi in 1838 as Francesco, son of Sante Possenti, he was baptised on his birth day and schooled by the Christian Brothers and Jesuits at Spoleto. After finishing secular study he joined the Passionists in 1856.

Clothed in the habit as Gabriel of Our Lady of Sorrows, he lived a short, intense religious life at Isola di Gran Sasso, dying in 1862 at twenty-three. Miracles reported at his tomb spread his fame. The entry presents a young student whose brief life became a model of devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-andre: Blessed Andrea Dotti, a Servite friar, was born in 1256 at Borgo San Sepolcro in Tuscany and died there in 1315. Brother of Count Dotto Dotti, captain of Philip the Fair's bodyguard archers, Andrea grew up a nobleman noted for piety and courage in the field. In 1278 a sermon by St. Philip Benizi at the Servite general chapter moved him to ask for the habit at once, and he rose by piety and learning in the order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-colom:
Blessed Colomba of Rieti, a Dominican mystic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Rieti in Umbria in 1467, she died at Perugia in 1501, spending most of her life away from her birthplace. Her fame rested on two things: the highly miraculous cast of her career from its start, and her deep love for the Blessed Sacrament.

She belongs to a band of saintly Dominican women raised up, the entry says, as a contrast to the irreligion of Renaissance Italy. Visions, fasting, and counsel to cities marked her short life. The entry presents a young woman whose holiness challenged a corrupt age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capuciati:
Capuciati takes its name from the caputium, or hood, worn as a mark by two very different groups. The first was a short-lived peace confraternity founded in France in 1182 or 1183. Durand, a poor carpenter from Le Puy, claimed a vision of the Virgin Mary, who gave him a picture and inscription calling for peace. Members bound themselves to keep and procure peace, wearing a white hood and a medal with the image.

Centered at Our Lady's church in Le Puy, the movement spread swiftly south of the Loire before fading. The same name later marked a class of English Lollards who followed the preaching of Peter Pateshull around 1387. They kept their hoods on before the Blessed Sacrament, a gesture of defiance that gave them the old name in a new cause.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-giusepp:
Carlo Giuseppe Imbonati was a Cistercian of the Reform of St. Bernard, an orientalist, biographer, and theologian born at Milan. He flourished in the later seventeenth century, and his death date is disputed, though it certainly fell no earlier than 1696. He held the chairs of theology and Hebrew at Rome and rose to abbot, after studying under Giulio Bartolocci of the same order.

Bartolocci had planned the great rabbinical library, and Imbonati, his pupil turned collaborator, finished and edited its fourth volume at Rome in 1693. A supplementary fifth volume followed in 1694, with a chronology of Scripture and two dissertations on the Messiah and on Christ's divinity and humanity. His tragic chronicle of princes, dated from the St. Bernard monastery in April 1696, gives the last firm date of his career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cayes-haiti:
Cayes is a Haitian diocese, suffragan to Port-au-Prince. The province of Port-au-Prince, with its archdiocese and four suffragan dioceses, dates only from the reorganization after the Concordat of 1860. That agreement joined Pius IX and Haiti. Yet the faith had been planted in this part of Santo Domingo toward the end of the fifteenth century. Despite the island's political and social upheavals, it was never quite extinguished there.

The Bishop of Cayes, Jean-Marie-Alexandre Morice, elected in March 1893, governed the whole civil Department of the South from his see at Cayes, a seaport in the island's extreme southwest. The diocese counted 25 parishes with 500,000 people, almost all Catholics by profession, and in 1907 it held 95 churches or chapels served by 35 secular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-celestino-sfo:
Celestino Sfondrati was prince-abbot of St. Gall and cardinal, born at Milan on 10 January 1644 and dying at Rome on 4 September 1696. He belonged to the noble Milanese Sfondrati family, which also produced Pope Gregory XIV and Cardinals Francesco and Paolo Sfondrati. At twelve he entered the Benedictine school at Rorschach, and on 26 April 1660 he took the habit at St. Gall.

By twenty-two he was already teaching philosophy and theology at Kempten. After ordination in 1668 he taught as professor and guided novices at his monastery. He taught canon law at Salzburg from 1679 to 1682, accepted the bishopric of Novara only with reluctance in 1686, and was instead elected prince-abbot of St. Gall in 1687. As abbot he modeled piety and mortification, and as prince he ruled mildly and won his people by great charity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chieti:
The Archdiocese of Chieti, ancient Teate, capital of the Marrucini, stands on a mountain above the River Pescara in the Abruzzi of central Italy. Its people, once enemies of Rome, made a league with the Romans in 304 before Christ. They became a municipality after the Allied War and passed through Goths, Lombards, and Normans into the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. Saint Justinus is honoured as the first bishop, and the cathedral bears his name.

Among later bishops, Giovanni Pietro Caraffa resigned the see in 1524 to found the Theatine Order with Saint Cajetan, and later became Pope Paul the Fourth. Since 1525 Chieti has been an archbishopric without suffragans, or subordinate dioceses. It counts 300,500 people, 113 parishes, and 442 churches and chapels. Its clergy number 170 secular and 58 regular priests, and the bronze doors at Saint Clement's still show Bishop Gribaldus of 874.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cincinnati:
An entry on the Archdiocese of Cincinnati, covering southern Ohio across 12,043 square miles, erected as a see in June 1821 and raised to an archdiocese in July 1850. Jesuits crossed Ohio as early as 1749, a mission rose at Sandusky in 1751, and French settlers built a church at Gallipolis in 1790. Bishop Flaget of Bardstown, touring northern Ohio with Father Badin, found the first Catholics at Somerset and called the Dominicans to their aid.

Father Fenwick, later the first Bishop of Cincinnati, first offered Mass for thirteen families in John Fink's house at Somerset. He secured three hundred acres from the Dittoe family for a Dominican church and monastery. John Baptist Purcell, consecrated second bishop in October 1833, built a cathedral and seminary as numbers grew. William Henry Elder succeeded in 1880, Henry Moeller followed as coadjutor in 1903, and by Elder's death in 1904 the see counted 180,000 Catholics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coluccio-di-p:
Paul Lejay's entry follows Coluccio di Pierio di Salutati, an Italian humanist born in Tuscany in 1331 and dead on 4 May 1406. He studied at Bologna, then went to Rome to serve as pontifical secretary to Urban IV. He loved ancient letters. From 1368 he wrote to Petrarch. In 1375 Florence called him as chancellor of the republic. He held that office until his death. His life filled with politics, and he wrote against the Duke of Milan.

Salutati's learning also shaped the young. He met scholars at San Spirito convent and at the Alberti villa of Paradiso, around Luigi de' Marsiglii. He guided young men well, treating Poggio as a son and protecting Bruni. His works include short treatises on fate and fortune and on religion and flight from the world. Only De nobilitate legum et medicinae reached print, at Venice. His letters and learning mark a bridge to the Renaissance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniele-farla:
A biographical entry presents Daniele Farlati, an ecclesiastical historian born at San Daniele del Friuli in 1690 and dead in 1773. Schooled at Gorz, he joined the Jesuits at Bologna in 1707, taught classics at Padua for five years, and was ordained at Rome in 1722. Sent back to Padua, he assisted Filippo Riceputi on a planned ecclesiastical history of Illyria.

For twenty years the pair searched libraries and archives of ancient Illyria, filling three hundred manuscript volumes. Riceputi died in 1712, just as two large sections neared completion, leaving Farlati alone to shape the mass. With Jacopo Coleti as helper, he issued the first volume of Illyricum Sacrum at Venice in 1751. Three more followed before his death, and Coleti completed the eight-folio work in 1818.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-domenico-feti:
Domenico Feti was an Italian painter born at Rome in 1589 who died at Venice in 1624. He studied under Cigoli, or at least felt that master's pull during his Roman years. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets him in the Rome of the jubilee year 1600, when the city again became the metropolis of beauty after the sack of 1527. Artists crowded thither, and the Carracci, Caravaggio, Domenichino, and Guido all worked there.

Between 1600 and 1610 even Rubens paid three visits to Rome, and Feti painted amid this brilliant company. His short life ended at thirty-five, yet his pictures hold a place in the Roman school of his day. The entry cites Lanzi, Blanc, and Burckhardt among the writers who judged his work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-corp:
Corpus Christi honours the institution of the Holy Eucharist each year. It falls on the Thursday after Trinity Sunday in the Latin Church. St Juliana of Mont Cornillon longed for such a feast from her youth. A vision of the moon with one dark spot strengthened her desire.

The bishop of Liege ordered the feast in 1246, and Urban IV spread it. His bull Transiturus of 1264 fixed the Thursday observance worldwide. Thomas Aquinas composed its Office, admired even by Protestants. The procession with the Host became a beloved hallmark of the day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-bra:
Francesco Brancati, born in Sicily in 1607, entered the Society of Jesus in 1624 and went to the Chinese missions in 1637. There he laboured for nearly thirty years in the province of Kiang-nan. He is said to have built more than ninety churches and forty-five chapels, and in 1665 he was exiled from Peking to Canton, where he died in 1671. His missionary career belongs to the heroic age of the Jesuit China mission, when a handful of Europeans preached across a vast empire.

Brancati wrote and published books in Chinese, most of them reprinted by Jesuit missionaries in the nineteenth century. They include a treatise on the Eucharist, instructions on the Decalogue and the Commandments of the Church, a refutation of divination. Sermons for Sundays and feast days and a catechism called Conversations of the Angels complete the list. His work on Chinese rites appeared in two volumes at Paris in 1700.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-chi:
Francesco Chieregati, born at Vicenza in 1479 and dead at Bologna on 6 December 1539, was a papal nuncio, or ambassador, whose career crossed the early Reformation.

There Chieregati had two tasks: to win German princes for war against the Turks in Hungary, and to enforce the Edict of Worms against Luther. In speeches of November and December he pressed both. On 3 January 1523 he read a papal brief in which Adrian frankly confessed abuses in Rome, a confession later writers have both blamed and praised. The German prelates, the entry says, were too timid and selfish to answer in kind, and the moment for a genuine reformation slipped away.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frascati:
Frascati, the ancient Tusculum, is one of the six suburbicarian dioceses, the sees neighbouring Rome and closely tied to the Roman Church from time immemorial. The city lies about twelve miles from Rome on the northern slopes of the Alban Hills, pleasantly and wholesomely placed. Its chief wealth is the vineyards that yield an excellent wine, with a population of ten thousand. Legend says Telegonus, son of Ulysses and Circe, founded Tusculum, ally of Rome in the kingly period and later subject to it.

 While other Latin towns waned, Tusculum grew into the favourite pleasure resort of rich Roman nobles, whose sumptuous villas, including Lucullus's, now Villa Torlonia, still dot the slopes among ruins. The diocese counts eight parishes and sixteen thousand souls, with nine houses for men, among them Grottaferrata Abbey and a Camaldolese monastery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gabriele-pale:
Gabriele Paleotti, cardinal and archbishop of Bologna, carried Trent's reforms into his diocese with the zeal of Borromeo at Milan. Born at Bologna in 1522, he took doctorates in civil and canon law in 1546, taught law, and became auditor of the Rota in 1556. Pius IV dispatched him to Trent's council, where his diary of the sessions remains a chief source for its history.

Made cardinal in 1565 and bishop of Bologna in 1567, Paleotti became its first archbishop when the see rose in rank in 1582. His biographers praise his drive to plant Tridentine reform at Bologna, and Borromeo himself held him high. His books treat sacred and profane images, the good rule of a diocese, and the blessing of old age, alongside a work on illegitimate children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-margo:
Giacomo Margotti was a Catholic journalist born at San Remo in 1823, who died in 1887. After studying classics, philosophy, and theology, and taking a doctorate at Genoa in 1845, he helped found the daily paper L'Armonia in 1848. A Catholic Encyclopedia article calls him the paper's soul and managing editor, feared for brilliant polemics against anti-Church laws in Sardinia.

Trials, fines, and plots followed his writing, and Cavour suppressed L'Armonia in 1859. It later returned and, at Pius IX's wish, took the name L'Unità Cattolica in December 1863. For years his judgment carried oracle weight among Italian Catholics, and he pressed the line of neither voting nor standing for election, in step with Pius IX. He left nearly 100,000 lire to charity, besides books on church and state and on the early years of Pius IX.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gian-matteo-g:
Gian Matteo Giberti was a cardinal and Bishop of Verona, born at Palermo in 1495 and dead at Verona in 1543. The natural son of a Genoese naval captain, he rose in the household of Cardinal Giulio de' Medici and became the cardinal's secretary. Clement VII made him Datario in 1523 and Bishop of Verona in 1524. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him from papal politics to diocesan reform.

He pushed the League of Cognac in 1526, was taken hostage in the sack of Rome in 1527, and escaped to Verona in 1528. There he set about reforming a clergy in poor shape. He printed Greek Fathers on his own press, reformed the choir school, and issued a catechism for the young. St. Charles Borromeo later studied his Verona system before taking up Milan, a mark of how far his reforms had run ahead of Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovani-devot:
Giovanni Devoti was a canon lawyer born at Rome in 1744, who died there in 1820. At twenty he held a chair of canon law at the Sapienza, where he taught for twenty-five years. Pius VI then made him Bishop of Anagni, a see he resigned in 1804 to become titular Archbishop of Carthage. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him through important Roman posts and exile with Pius VII in France.

His works include an early study of the best-known laws of 1766 and a vast canon law in five planned books, of which only three volumes appeared. His clearest book, the four-volume Institutions of 1785, won praise for clearness, conciseness, and historical notes. Spain made it compulsory at Alcalá in 1817, and Louvain adopted it as a classic manual in 1836. Today it serves history more than practice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Viotti, founder of the modern school of violin playing, was born at Fontanetto in Piedmont in 1753, and died in 1824. He studied under Giovannini and at Turin under Pugnani, touring with him in 1780. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a virtuoso whose playing won attention in Germany, Russia, and France.

Attached for a time to the court of Marie Antoinette, he left Paris in the Revolution and reached London in July 1792. He led at the King's Theatre and stood in the highest esteem as a teacher, left England in 1798 over intrigue, and returned in 1801. After a failed venture as a wine merchant, he directed the French Opera from 1819 to 1822. His concertos and sonatas enriched violin music, and pupils like Rode carried his manner on.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-lore:
Giovanni Lorenzo Berti was an Italian theologian born at Sarravezza in Tuscany in 1696, who died at Pisa in 1766. Of humble parents, he entered the Augustinians at fifteen and preached with success before twenty-three. He taught philosophy and theology at Siena, Florence, Bologna, Padua, and Rome, and in 1748 became professor of church history at Pisa. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an agitated literary career.

At his superior general's order he wrote De Theologicis Disciplinis, an exposition of St. Augustine's teaching, published at Rome between 1739 and 1745. Attackers charged him with Jansenism, and he answered with defenses of the Augustinian system of grace. Benedict XIV had the book examined and found its teaching sound. Berti also wrote a life of St. Augustine, a history of the first three centuries' heresies, and a church history often reprinted.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-paol:
Giovanni Paolo Lancelotti was a canonist born at Perugia in 1522, who died there in 1590. He took his doctorate in law in 1546 and taught at his native university from 1547 or 1548. Except for two short stays at Rome, he spent his life at Perugia in law and letters. A Catholic Encyclopedia article owes his world-wide fame to one small book.

His Institutiones Juris Canonici, published at Perugia in 1563 as a private venture, copied Justinian's plan for an elementary Roman law textbook. In four books it treats persons, things above all marriage, judgments, and crimes, a division later elementary writers followed. Paul IV had charged him with the work in 1557, but neither Paul IV nor Pius IV gave it official approval, and it predates the Council of Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girgenti:
Girgenti is a diocese in Sicily, its capital a city about three miles from the sea on a steep rock above a rich plain watered by the Drago. The Greeks called it Acragas and the Romans Agrigentum, founded by a colony from Gela about 582 BC. Besides trade in vegetables, fruits, and cereals, it mines sulphur, soda, chalk, copper, and iron. A Catholic Encyclopedia article surveys its ancient splendor and its later church history.

After Syracuse it ranked as the first town in Sicily, rich in trade with Carthage, but often ruled by tyrants. Carthaginians sacked it in 406. Romans took it in 262 and held it fully from 210. Its ruins still testify to its wealth, above all the Temple of Concord, best preserved because later used as a church. The temple of Olympian Jove was called by Polybius the largest and most beautiful in Sicily.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-gius:
Giuseppe Giusti was a poet and patriot born in 1809 at Monsumano near Pescia in Italy, who died on 31 March 1850 at Florence. Trained by a private tutor and an academy at Florence, he studied law at Pisa and took his degree in 1834, delayed in part by a political satire that displeased the authorities. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a lyric voice turned satirist of Italy's abuses.

Settled at Florence ostensibly to practice law, he gave himself to letters. His early lyrics, called scherzi, spread in manuscript before their sanctioned publication at Leghorn in 1844. He began under Petrarch's influence, then found a romantic and elegiac strain of his own. His political satires, in varied lyric measures, picture Italy in his day, attack social abuses, and long for political and moral renewal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-mezz:
Giuseppe Mezzofanti was a cardinal and the greatest of polyglots, born on 19 September 1774, who died on 15 March 1849. Son of a poor carpenter of Bologna, he learned Spanish, German, Mexican, and some South American dialects from ex-Jesuits exiled from America. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a memory so prodigious that at twelve he began a three-year course of philosophy.

In 1797 he took the chair of Hebrew at Bologna and was ordained priest. He then lost his chair for refusing the oath to the Cisalpine Republic. Tending wounded soldiers of many nations in the hospitals of Bologna in 1799 and 1800, he perfected old languages and learned new ones. Called to Rome in 1831, he placed his learning at the service of the Holy See, becoming Domestic Prelate and canon of Saint Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-graffiti:
Graffiti is the term archaeologists use for rude inscriptions scratched on the walls of ancient monuments, generally sepulchral, as distinct from formal inscriptions engraved on tombs. A Catholic Encyclopedia article shows how pilgrim scratches guided De Rossi through the Roman catacombs.

Traced by pilgrims between the fourth and ninth centuries on gallery walls, the graffiti proved invaluable. Their absence meant nothing important nearby, while their presence meant an important crypt or martyr's tomb at hand. Pilgrims scratched names, dates, or prayers, such as the appeal to Saint Sixtus to remember Aurelius Repentinus. Outside the catacombs, the Palatine caricature of the Crucifixion mocks the page Alexamenos adoring his God, while a second inscription proclaims him a Christian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haiti:
Haiti, the western republic on the island Columbus reached in December 1492, is surveyed here in statistics, politics, and mission history. The island divides into Spanish Santo Domingo in the east and Haiti in the west. It has 11,070 square miles and 1,579,630 people in 1909, coffee, sugar, cotton, and tobacco as chief products, and a Catholic faith still mixed with African Voodoo.

French settlement from 1659, Toussaint L'Ouverture's rising, Dessalines's massacre and empire, Christophe's northern kingdom, and a string of troubled presidents fill the political half. Mission history runs from the dioceses of 1511 through Dominicans, Capuchins, and Jesuits, the Revolution's wreckage, and the concordat of March 1860 that put the Church under government protection with salaried clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helena-tarabo:
Venetian nun Helena Tarabotti, called Arcangela in religion, was forced by her father into St. Anna's convent at eleven without a vocation and became an author of note through study. Born in 1605 and dead in 1652, she found her element in earnest reading. Her early books show an unsettled mind before Cardinal Cornaro's influence brought her peace in treatises on the spiritual life.

Her worldly works, some under the pen name Galerana Barcitotti, answer a satire on women's luxury, defend women against Orazio Plata, and unmask simplicity deceived, with familiar letters of 1650 beside them. Spiritual books on monastic light, the road to heaven, monastic paradise, the purgatory of ill-married women, and contemplations of the loving soul complete a life spent, willingly or not, behind convent walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-humiliati:
The Humiliati were a penitential order dating, by some accounts, to the early eleventh century, but more probably to the early twelfth, under Emperor Henry V. After quelling a Lombard rebellion, Henry led captive nobles to Germany, where, converted from worldly vanities, they took grey penitential garb and works of charity and mortification. On pledging loyalty, they returned to Lombardy.

Called Barettini from their head-dress, they knew German woollen making and brought improved methods to Italy, boosting the industry, employing the poor, and sharing gains with the needy. On Bernard's advice in 1134, many withdrew from the world with their wives' consent and founded their first monastery at Milan, exchanging grey for white. Later, on John Meda's advice, they took the Rule of Benedict adapted to their needs and won papal approval.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignazio-danti:
Ignazio Danti was a mathematician and cosmographer, born at Perugia in 1537 and dead at Alatri in 1586. His father and aunt taught the boy painting and architecture first, yet numbers and science drew him most. In 1555 he took the Dominican habit and swapped his baptismal name Pellegrino for Ignazio.

Philosophy and theology done, he preached for a while, then threw himself into mathematics, astronomy, and geography. Around 1567, Tuscany's Cosmo I called him to Florence to breathe new life into mathematics and astronomy there. His mathematics teaching won great success and arguably cleared the path for Galileo and his peers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-illuminati:
Members of a secret society started by Adam Weishaupt in 1776 called themselves the Illuminati. Weishaupt, born at Ingolstadt in 1748 to Westphalian parents, lost his father when he was five. A Jesuit school educated him, yet his free-thinking godfather shaped him early. That man ran the Ickstatt high school and got Weishaupt his Ingolstadt professorship in civil law in 1772.

A year later Weishaupt became the first lay holder of Ingolstadt's canon-law chair. His rationalist sway over students, both in lectures and in private talk, set him increasingly at odds with devoted Catholics and with men in government. Quarrelsome by temper, he clashed with nearly everyone he knew well. So he wanted a strong secret body behind him, to back him against enemies and to push his rationalist plans for Church and state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-faccio:
Lexicographer Jacopo Facciolati was born at Torreglia near Padua on 4 January 1682. He died at Padua on 26 August 1769. He was educated at Padua seminary. Later he became professor of logic at Padua university. He also served as regent of the schools there for forty-five years. In 1719 he issued a revised Calepinus, a Latin dictionary in seven languages.

His pupil Forcellini assisted him on that work. Their labors convinced them that Latin needed a wholly new lexicon. So they set aside all other work and began the largest Latin vocabulary ever made. For forty years Forcellini labored under Facciolati's supervision. He read through the entire body of Latin literature. The entry presents a teacher whose dictionary project outlived his own long career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-piccol:
Cardinal Jacopo Piccolomini Ammannati was born near Lucca in 1422. He died near Bolsena on 10 September 1479. He was related to Siena's Piccolomini family. He gained his literary and theological education at Florence. Under Nicholas V he went to Rome and lived for a time in extreme poverty. In 1450 he became private secretary to Cardinal Domenico Capranica.

Later Callistus III named him secretary of briefs. Pius II kept him in that office and made him a household member. On that occasion he took the Piccolomini name. In 1460 Pius II made him bishop of Pavia. Throughout that pontificate he served as trusted confidant and adviser. He governed his diocese with paternal care. During long absences he left its affairs to able vicars in constant touch. On 18 December 1461 he became cardinal. The entry follows a secretary risen to the sacred college.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-benedict:
Jean Benedicti, a sixteenth-century French Franciscan theologian of Tours and Poitiers, rose to secretary of his order and travelled Europe with its minister-general on visitations. He later served as commissary-general for France, visited Italian provinces, and made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land to fulfil a vow.

Benedicti mastered Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, and Wadding praised his learning and parts. His Sum of Sins and Their Remedy, first printed at Paris in 1599, became a confessor's handbook, reaching fifteen editions after Paris theologians revised it. He also wrote on a famed exorcism at Lyons, and was buried at the Laval friary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-m-fino:
Joseph M. Finotti was an Italian-born Jesuit and historian of American Catholic books. Born at Ferrara in 1817, he joined the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1833 and came to Maryland in 1845 with Father Ryder's recruits. After ordination at Georgetown he served at Alexandria, Virginia, then left the order in 1852 for Boston.

In Boston he edited The Pilot and served parishes at Brookline and Arlington, ending his life as pastor of Central City, Colorado. A great book lover, he wrote lives of saints and translated works for American readers. His unfinished Bibliographica Catholica Americana aimed to catalogue every Catholic book published in the United States, with notes on authors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-tomas-de:
Juan Tomás de Rocaberti was a Spanish Dominican who defended papal primacy in twenty-one volumes. Born about 1624 at Perelada, he joined the Dominicans at Gerona in 1640, taught theology at Valencia, and was elected general of his order in 1670. Charles II made him Archbishop of Valencia in 1676 and governor of the province, then Inquisitor-General of Spain in 1695.

Rocaberti won the canonization of Louis Bertrand and Rose of Lima and the beatification of Pius V. His De Romani pontificis auctoritate of 1691 to 1694 opened his defense of Rome against Gallicans and Protestants. His Bibliotheca Maxima Pontificia, published at Rome from 1697 to 1700, gathers in full every major orthodox work on the primacy, from Bzovius to Boverius.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lancelot-poli:
Lancelot Politi, in religion Ambrosius Catharinus (1483-1553), was a Sienese Dominican theologian, doctor of civil and canon law at sixteen and professor at Siena from 1508. His pupils included Giovanni del Monte, later Julius III, and Sixtus of Siena.

Entering the Dominicans at Florence about 1513, he studied Scripture and theology alone, which bred his independence on predestination, assurance of grace, bishops' residence, and sacramental intention. A fierce defender against Luther, he spoke notably at Trent's third public session in February 1546. Made Bishop of Minori in 1546 and Archbishop of Conza in 1552, he died bound for Rome. Julius III meant to make him cardinal. He was praised as brilliant and eccentric yet always orthodox.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leandro-alber:
Leandro Alberti (1479 to probably 1552) was a Bolognese Dominican historian, tutored in youth by the rhetorician Giovanni Garzo and entering the Order in 1493. Called to Rome by Master General Francesco Silvestro Ferraris, he served as his secretary and companion until Ferraris died in 1528.

In 1517 he published a six-book treatise on famous men of his Order, reprinted countless times and translated widely. He also wrote saints' lives, a history of the Madonna di San Luca, and a Bologna chronicle to 1273. Caccianemici continued it to 1279. His fame rests chiefly on the Descrizione d'Italia of 1550, rich in topography and archaeology but weak where it follows Annius of Viterbo's uncritical work. He also chronicled events from 1499 to 1552 and knew the contents of most European libraries better than hardly any man of his day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leone-battist:
Leone Battista Alberti (1404-1472) was a fifteenth-century Florentine ecclesiastic and artist, best known by his architecture. Born 18 February 1404, he took the ecclesiastical state. He became a canon of Florence's Metropolitan Church in 1447 and Abbot of San Savino, or Sant' Eremita, of Pisa. Scholar, painter, sculptor, and architect though he was, his buildings made his name.

They include the Pitti Palace's completion at Florence, the Rucellai chapel in St. Pancras, the facade of Santa Maria Novella, the Nunziata choir, and the Mantuan churches of St. Sebastian and St. Andrew. His greatest work is generally the church of St. Francis at Rimini. On art, his writings rank as his best. His reputation rests largely on De Re Aedificatoria, a ten-volume work on architecture published only after his death, in 1485, with a folio edition at Bologna in 1782.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-di-ci:
Lorenzo Ghiberti was the Florentine bronze sculptor who opened the early Renaissance in sculpture, born about 1381 and dead in 1455. In 1401 he beat Brunelleschi and others for the north bronze doors of the baptistery, with a Sacrifice of Isaac panel still kept in Florence.

Those doors, finished between 1403 and 1424, hold twenty-eight panels in quatrefoil frames: twenty scenes from Christ's life above, evangelists and Fathers below. His eastern doors took ten Old Testament scenes and finished in 1452, with crowds, landscapes, and deep perspective that made sculpture rival painting. Both doors still draw study for their craft and storytelling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-tosti:
Luigi Tosti was a Benedictine historian, born at Naples in 1811 and dead at Monte Cassino in 1897. Left fatherless young, he was raised by a monk uncle, entered Monte Cassino as a pupil in 1819, was ordained in 1833, and taught Thomas Aquinas there for twenty years.

From 1842 his histories poured out: Monte Cassino abbey, Boniface VIII, the Lombard League of 1848, Abelard, Constance, the Greek schism, Matilda, and prolegomena to a universal church history. He backed Pius IX's national movement, planned a review to put the papacy atop the Risorgimento, and was jailed on a false conspiracy charge until the pope freed him. His Ricordi biblici grew from that ordeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lumen-christi:
Lumen Christi, Light of Christ, is the versicle sung by the deacon on Holy Saturday while he kindles the triple candle. New fire is blessed outside the church, an acolyte carries a light in, and the procession climbs the nave with the deacon in white bearing three candles.

Three times the train halts. The deacon lights one candle and sings Lumen Christi on one note, falling a third on the final syllable. The choir replies Deo gratias, thanks be to God, each time higher, and all kneel. At the altar the Exultet blessing of the Paschal Candle follows. Triple candles began as a guard against wind, and only later gathered their symbolism of three.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-michelangelo-:
Michelangelo Buonarroti, Italian sculptor, painter, and architect, was born at Caprese in the upper Arno valley on 6 March 1475 and died at Rome on 18 February 1564. Sprung from a noble Florentine family of small means, he was apprenticed in 1488 to Domenico Ghirlandajo. As apprentice he stirred his master's wonder with the lifelike animation of his drawings. On Ghirlandajo's word, and at Lorenzo the Magnificent's wish, he trained from 1489 to 1492 in the Medici palace school of sculpture under Bertoldo, a Donatello pupil.

Living in the palace with Lorenzo's sons, Michelangelo was led by the poet Politian into the Academy scholars' circle. After Lorenzo's death he divided his time between home, Santo Spirito monastery, where he pursued anatomy, and Pietro de' Medici's house, until Pietro's banishment in 1494. About then Michelangelo left Florence for Bologna, returning in 1495 to work as a sculptor, modelling himself on predecessors and classical masterpieces without surrendering his own stamp.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-musti:
Musti was a titular see of Proconsular Africa, suffragan to Carthage, an early Roman municipium. It is named by Ptolemy, the Antonine Itinerary, the Peutinger Table and the Ravenna geographer, who tells of Regulus killing an enormous serpent there. Its ruins, called Mest Henshir, lie near the shrine of Sidi Abd-er-Rehou between Teboursouk and Keff in Tunis, with two fine gates and a triumphal arch.

Inscriptions call its people Musticenses or Mustitani, the latter used by Saint Augustine. At the Carthage conference of 411 Musti fielded two Donatist bishops, Feicianus and Cresconius, and two Catholic bishops, Victorianus and Leontius. Antonianus was exiled by Huneric in 482, and Bishop Januarius signed the 646 letter against the Monothelites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-niccolo-alber:
Bologna gave Niccolo Albergati birth in 1357; he died at Siena on 9 May 1443, a Cardinal and Bishop of Bologna. He took Carthusian vows in 1394, led several monasteries as prior, and took the Bologna bishopric unwillingly in 1417. As bishop he kept his Order's Rule, pressed for reform among regular and secular clergy, and backed learned men with generous support, Aeneas Sylvius, later Pius II, among them.

Popes Martin V and Eugenius IV sent him on weighty errands, three times to France in 1422, 1431, and 1435, and three times to Lombardy in 1426, 1427, and 1430. He rose to cardinal in 1426. At Basel in 1432, 1434, and 1436 he acted as Eugenius's legate, and at Ferrara in 1438 after the synod shifted there. He sat in Greek union talks ahead of Florence, and took the Grand Penitentiary's post not long before he died. Though never formally canonised, he has long been honoured by the people as Blessed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicola-arrigh:
Florentine scholar Nicola Arrighetti, a pupil of Galileo, combined mathematics, philosophy, and letters in seventeenth-century Florence. He held a leading place in the Florentine Academy and the Academy of Della Crusca, and helped refound the Platonic Academy under the grand duke.

Arrighetti gave its opening address and was turning Plato's dialogues into Tuscan when he died in 1639. Many manuscripts survive, with prose and verse on topics as varied as the tortoise, the cucumber, and pickles. He pronounced the opening discourse when the grand duke and the prince re-established the Platonic Academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicola-coleti:
Venetian priest and historian Nicola Coleti devoted his career to gathering and correcting the records of church councils. Born at Venice in 1680 and trained at Padua, he first reworked Ughelli's Italia Sacra in ten volumes, fixing errors and carrying its story into the eighteenth century.

His larger project, a collection of council documents published by his brother at Venice from 1728 to 1733, ran to twenty-three volumes. Its two index volumes made it especially prized, and Coleti added further histories of bishops and Venetian church monuments. He also annotated a manuscript of Maffei now kept in the Vallicellana Library at Rome.
